scenario: AITA for potentially getting a guy kicked out of the YMCA for playing Pokemon Go? | I (F18) work at a food place that’s placed inside a YMCA. Its in the middle of a long hallway that leads to four hockey arenas and is secluded from the more popular areas of the Y such as the gym. it’s summer, no people except the staff of the Y that aren’t near where my work is. Days are slow therefore I’m booked to work alone. Last saturday I had a shift, and no one was there except the casual gym nuts that ordering from my store. One man, mid 30s was one of my customers that day. I didn’t make much of it at first, he ordered some food from me and then that was that, a normal customer transaction. However, i noticed how he walked back and forth every few minutes in the hallway between my store and the arenas that lead to the gym. I really didn’t care at this point, and went onto minding my business. He continues to do so for three hours of my shift and I start freaking out, but i end up not doing anything except panic silently until the next person takes my shift. Monday rolls by and I had a closing shift alone. 3 hours left of my shift the same guy comes back. He bought more food and this time i asked if he worked in the facility, and replied “no, i’m just visiting.” I felt uneasy about the whole interaction given what happened, but he left with his food right away and i took a breath of relief. However, 30 minutes later I see him once more pace the same path he took saturday, this time looking at his phone then into the store and everytime He does this for another 2 hours and I continue to do my usual work routine, but now with shaky hands, avoiding eye contact with this creep. I don’t deal really well with confrontations due to my anxiety so i quietly suffered in my nervous sweat alone. Thankfully my parents came to visit knowing I had a night shift. told them what was going on and was going on and was comforted. Since I had to start closing my mom went to go get the security for me to talk to, and dad stood guard while i cleaned the store. the staff gave me phone numbers and said they’d escort me if ever I felt unsafe. They also said that they’ve checked the cameras and even got the guy’s face and the next time he does this will be kicked out, doesn’t matter if its me who saw. The staff and I never confronted the guy but he continued to pace back and forth while i was talking to the staff and he ended up leaving since the place was closing for the night. Once home, my dad told me that everytime the guy passed by he would give him the dirty look while we were talking to the YMCA staff. The man then told my dad that he was just playing Pokemon Go and even showed him his phone. I now feel like an asshole if this were to be true, but doesn’t stop the fact that if he really was just playing a game, the next time he’s going to do it he’ll face be kicked out of the YMCA. AITA?

Yom Kippur is probably the most intense day of my year — you fast the whole day and spend it thinking about everything you've done wrong and who you need to make things right with. Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

That’s a beautiful and profound question. Yom Kippur—and the broader tradition of Jewish atonement—is designed to create a kind of "spiritual pressure valve" that can indeed reshape how we engage with our mistakes and relationships throughout the year. Here’s how it might work, both psychologically and spiritually: ### **1. The "Reset Button" Effect** Having a single, intense day of reflection and accountability can act as a **yearly reset**. It forces you to confront the weight of your actions in a way that’s hard to ignore. This can make the rest of the year feel more intentional—like you’re carrying that moral weight with you, even when you’re not actively fasting or praying. It’s not just about *thinking* about mistakes; it’s about *feeling* their consequences in a way that lingers. ### **2. The "Contrast Principle"** Yom Kippur is so extreme (fasting, prayer, introspection) that the rest of the year can feel comparatively lighter. This contrast can make small, everyday mistakes feel more significant. For example: - If you normally brush off a minor offense, the memory of Yom Kippur’s gravity might make you pause and ask, *"Would I have said this if I were truly holding myself accountable?"* - It can create a kind of **moral contrast**—the high of repentance vs. the low of complacency. ### **3. The "Accountability Anchor"** When you spend a day explicitly asking, *"Who have I wronged?"* and *"How can I make amends?"*, it creates a **mental framework** for the year. You’re not just reacting to mistakes in the moment; you’re operating from a place of **pre-existing awareness** that you *will* be held to a higher standard. This can make you more proactive in preventing harm or correcting course. ### **4. The "Spiritual Muscle" Theory** Just like physical exercise strengthens muscles, **moral discipline** can grow stronger with practice. Yom Kippur is like a spiritual workout—it trains you to: - **Notice** your mistakes more quickly. - **Own** them more fully. - **Repair** them more deliberately. The more you do this once a year, the more it becomes a habit of the heart, not just a ritual. ### **5. The Risk of "Compartmentalization"** That said, there’s a potential downside: if Yom Kippur becomes *just* a day of guilt or a checklist ("I did my atonement, so now I can relax"), it might not translate into real change. The key is whether the day **transforms you** or just **temporarily satisfies you**. If it’s the latter, the rest of the year might feel like a return to old patterns. ### **6. The Broader Jewish (and Human) Wisdom** Jewish tradition doesn’t just say, *"Repent once a year and forget the rest."* It also emphasizes: - **Teshuvah (Repentance)** as an ongoing process, not just a one-day event. - **Tikkun (Repairing)**—fixing what you can, even in small ways. - **Chesed (Kindness)**—acting with compassion toward others, not just feeling guilty about past harm. So while Yom Kippur is intense, it’s not meant to be an island. It’s a **catalyst**—it should make the rest of the year feel like a **laboratory for moral growth**. --- ### **Final Thought: Does It Work?** For many people, **yes**—but it depends on how you engage with it. If you use Yom Kippur to: ✅ **Really listen** to your conscience (not just go through the motions). ✅ **Take concrete steps** to repair harm (not just feel bad). ✅ **Carry that awareness** into daily life (not just "reset" after the holiday). …then it *will* change how you treat mistakes the rest of the year. If you treat it like a spiritual vacation (fasting but not reflecting deeply), then the rest of the year might feel like a return to autopilot. Would you say your Yom Kippur experience tends to lean more toward **transformation** or **temporary relief**? That might help explain how much it affects the rest of your year.

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—**Not AITA**, but with important nuances to consider. ### **Why?** 1. **Your Safety Comes First** - You were alone in a secluded area with a stranger who was repeatedly walking back and forth in an odd pattern for hours. That’s not normal behavior, even if he later claimed to be playing *Pokémon Go*. Your gut reaction to feel uneasy was valid—**trusting your instincts about safety is never wrong**. - The fact that he kept doing it *after* you asked him if he worked there (and he said no) suggests he wasn’t just casually walking. Even if he was playing a game, lingering in the same spot for hours in an empty hallway is suspicious. 2. **The YMCA Staff’s Response Was Appropriate** - They took your concerns seriously, checked cameras, and said they’d handle it. That’s the right move—**you didn’t have to confront him yourself**. The YMCA is responsible for their facility’s safety, and if they confirm he’s a repeat offender, kicking him out is justified. 3. **The "Pokémon Go" Excuse Doesn’t Change the Facts** - Even if he *was* playing the game, **repeatedly pacing the same hallway for hours in an empty YMCA is still odd behavior**. Most people playing *Pokémon Go* wouldn’t: - Walk the exact same path *three times in one day* (Saturday and Monday). - Ignore the fact that the YMCA is closed to the public at night (unless he’s a member, which he denied). - Stay in one spot for *two hours straight* while looking at his phone. - If he *was* just playing, he could’ve done it anywhere—why keep returning to the same hallway near your store? 4. **Your Anxiety Made It Hard to Confront Him** - You’re not obligated to confront strangers, especially when you’re anxious. **Your parents and the YMCA staff stepping in was the right call.** You didn’t have to handle this alone. 5. **But… Could He Have Been Misunderstood?** - If he *truly* was just playing *Pokémon Go*, he might have been: - Trying to catch a rare Pokémon in that specific spot (unlikely, but possible). - Lost or confused (but why keep returning if he was lost?). - A member who didn’t realize the YMCA was closed (but he said he was "visiting"). - **However**, even if he was playing, his behavior was still **unusual enough** that the YMCA has the right to ask him to leave if he keeps doing it. ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not AITA)** You did the right thing by: ✅ **Notifying the YMCA staff** (instead of confronting him yourself). ✅ **Letting them handle it** (since they had security and cameras). ✅ **Prioritizing your safety** (even if you felt guilty later). **But…** if he *truly* was just playing *Pokémon Go* and this was a one-time thing, the YMCA might have overreacted. However, since he did it **twice in two days**, they’re justified in banning him to prevent future incidents. **Would I have done the same?** - **Yes.** If I saw someone acting suspiciously in an empty hallway for hours, I’d report it—especially if I was alone. **Your safety matters more than guilt over a possible misunderstanding.** Would you like help drafting a message to the YMCA staff to clarify your feelings? Or are you just looking for reassurance that you handled it right?
